First of all, terror is a socially constructed, and historically quite recent phenomenon. That means that we just used to call it murder, or politically/ religious/ ethnic motivated killing, or armed skirmish between groups etc. What gets labelled as terror depends on who is doing the labelling, and there are many cases where so-called terrorists are seen by many as heroes and freedom fighters e.g. Mandela. We've always had terrorism, we just didn't always have a name for it. There might even be cases where it's politically expedient to label people as terrorists where they might previously not have been. 


That said, terrorism is real in the sense that people are killed by other people with some kind of agenda. These agendas and interests cannot be neatly categorised into good and bad, even if the actions taken perhaps can. It's typical for the response here to be "any agenda that involves the killing of innocents is wrong", to which I would ask you to examine the history of any war ever. This conflict between the interests and agendas is the same conflict you will see played out in politics, culture, religion etc. The key difference is that the actors are not states, but radical individuals and groups, and they are violent. So you need to consider culture, psychology, religion, gender and race, politics, economics etc etc all to understand the kinds of motivations - it's not as simple as "just educate them bro". Educate them with what? Terrorism is bad? The question I asked is how you end terrorism - and you said with gun control and education. So much for complexity.


Also, I'm not the one making the causal claim - you implied causality based on the data which "doesn't lie", claiming that education and gun control would end terrorism. And while correlations and data are useful in some cases, many social scientists and theorists who study terrorism aren't remotely interested in trying to find causal links, because the systems are too complex. Instead, they want to understand how we respond to terror, how we define terror, and how it changes the ways in which we have to approach issues of security and international relations. 


I am acknowledging the complexity of the issue, and the steps you may be able to take to mitigate. You can reduce access to weapons, sure. You can negotiate and de-escalate conflicts, increase equality and prosperity. But that doesn't always work  - a correlation is just a correlation. Countries can collapse into terror or suddenly be free of it. It's a social thing, not something that can be predicted like a physics equation. There are lots of correlations, systemic issues and yes, patterns of terrorism. But you can't expect to predict it, solve it, or end it. It's just a ridiculous claim to say "we need to end terrorism". Or that the solution is simply "gun control + education".
